lesson.title: Straightening the Curve: Linearizing Rate Data to Find k and Order
lesson.summary: Formalizes the transformation technique for determining reaction order from data, with a worked second-order dataset that is tested against both first- and second-order linear forms.
lesson.body:
"Linearizing" rate data means algebraically transforming a table of (t, [A]) measurements into new coordinates that fall on a straight line only if you have identified the correct reaction order. This is not a new idea at this point in the unit, it is the direct graphical consequence of the three integrated rate laws already built. Zero order data is already linear in [A] versus t. First order data becomes linear once you plot ln[A] versus t, because ln[A] = ln[A]0 - kt is already in y = mx + b form. Second order data becomes linear once you plot 1/[A] versus t, because 1/[A] = 1/[A]0 + kt is likewise already in y = mx + b form. Each transformation is simply the rearranged integrated rate law for that order, nothing more mysterious than that.

The diagnostic workflow: given a table of concentration versus time, compute both ln[A] and 1/[A] for every data point, then check which of the two resulting columns has constant, equal differences between consecutive equal time intervals. Constant differences mean a straight line; unequal differences mean a curve, and that order is ruled out.

Worked example with a fresh dataset, second order this time, to complete the picture the previous section built with first order data:

t (min): 0, 10.0, 20.0
[A] (M): 0.400, 0.200, 0.1333

Test first order first, computing ln[A]:
ln(0.400) = -0.916
ln(0.200) = -1.609
ln(0.1333) = -2.015

The first interval changes by -1.609 - (-0.916) = -0.693 over 10.0 minutes, a rate of -0.0693 per minute. The second interval changes by -2.015 - (-1.609) = -0.406 over 10.0 minutes, a rate of -0.0406 per minute. These two slopes are not equal, so ln[A] versus t is not a straight line here, and first order is ruled out for this data.

Now test second order, computing 1/[A]:
1/0.400 = 2.50
1/0.200 = 5.00
1/0.1333 = 7.50

The first interval changes by 5.00 - 2.50 = 2.50 over 10.0 minutes, a slope of 0.250 M^-1 min^-1. The second interval changes by 7.50 - 5.00 = 2.50 over 10.0 minutes, the same slope of 0.250 M^-1 min^-1. These two slopes match exactly, confirming that 1/[A] versus t is a straight line, that this reaction is second order, and that its rate constant is k = 0.250 M^-1 min^-1, read directly off the slope.

This dataset is not a coincidence: it is the exact same second order reaction, same k and same [A]0, used to introduce the second order integrated rate law earlier in this unit, where 0.400 M was shown to drop to 0.200 M in 10.0 minutes. Seeing those same numbers reappear here, now used to prove the order rather than assume it, is the point: linearization is not a separate new idea, it is the graphical proof of the algebra learned earlier in this unit.

One practical note for real laboratory data: actual measurements always carry some experimental noise, so a real analysis uses a best fit line through many points (linear regression) rather than just two points, and judges "how straight" a line really is using a quantity like R^2, a statistic close to 1.00 for a well fit straight line. The two-point method shown above captures the core logic cleanly, but a genuine data set deserves the full line of best fit before drawing a firm conclusion about order.
